provenance: Opus 5.5 subscription CLI draft with host review/repairs, source restrictions and execution verification.

draft_notes.explanation: Each non-background colour is one solid rectangle. Rectangles may overlap, but the generator guarantees that two opposite corners of every rectangle stay visible. That makes the bounding box of a colour's visible pixels equal to its true rectangle. The emitted program measures each colour's bounding box in visible coordinates and picks the background. The background is the colour whose span exceeds 10 cells in some dimension, which no box can do; ties are broken by pixel count. It then sorts the rectangles by area, largest first. The output canvas has the largest rectangle's size and colour. Every remaining rectangle is stamped in decreasing area order, aligned to one fixed corner of the canvas. In the original task that corner is the top-left. Under the D4 map the corner moves to a known place: index 4 and above means a row reversal, which sends top-left to top-right. Each clockwise rotation then cycles top-left -> top-right -> bottom-right -> bottom-left. The factory turns this into the constant CORNER and slices the canvas directly at that corner. Bounding-box heights and widths are taken in visible coordinates, so rotations swap them naturally. Colours are used as observed, so no palette constants are needed.
draft_notes.limitations: Background detection assumes the background spans more than 10 cells in some direction, which follows from the generator (grid at least 14 per side, boxes at most 10 per side). Using the per-colour bounding box instead of connected components relies on the generator's corner-visibility guarantee; this is more robust than the archived solver when a rectangle is split by an overlapping one. Equal-area ties cannot occur under the generator, because box widths and heights are paired monotonically and duplicate size pairs are rejected. A deterministic tie-break is still included. The program has not been run or tested.
